Question: A point \(P\) is chosen at random in the interior of equilateral triangle \(ABC.\) What is the probability that \(\triangle ABP\) has a greater area than each of \(\triangle ACP\) and \(\triangle BCP?\)
Solution:
Interpret the random choice as uniform by area. A rotation of \(120^\circ\) about the center of the equilateral triangle carries \(A\) to \(B\), \(B\) to \(C\), and \(C\) to \(A\). It preserves areas and carries the triangle onto itself. Thus it cycles the three events that \(ABP\), \(BCP\), or \(CAP\) has strictly the greatest area. These three events therefore have equal probabilities.

We must also account for ties. Since \(AB=AC\), the area formula \(\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}\) shows that \(ABP\) and \(ACP\) have equal areas exactly when \(P\) has equal perpendicular distances to \(AB\) and \(AC\). Inside the triangle, such points lie on the angle bisector at \(A\). The other two possible pairwise ties similarly lie on the angle bisectors at \(B\) and \(C\).

These three line segments have zero area, so a uniformly chosen point lies on them with probability zero. Away from them, exactly one of the three areas is strictly greatest. The three equally probable, disjoint events consequently have total probability \(1\), making each probability \(\boxed{\frac13}\). The answer is choice C.
